summary: Provides guidelines for evaluating new congestion control algorithms for interactive point-to-point real-time media carried over RTP, as in telephony and video conferencing. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When someone invents a new way for video calls to avoid jamming the network, how do you know it works? This document describes how to measure and judge such ideas fairly.

questions: how to evaluate rtp congestion control
what makes a good real-time congestion control test
what network parameters should be used to test real-time congestion control
subtitle: Metrics, network settings and traffic models for testing new congestion control for interactive real-time media.

tldr.problem: New congestion control algorithms for interactive real-time media need to be tested in a comparable way, or their results cannot be trusted or compared.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines metrics, an RTP packet log format, ranges for delay, loss and queue length, a loss model and jitter models, and traffic models for TCP, RTP video and background UDP.
tldr.outcome: It supplies the building blocks for the test scenarios in RFC 8867 and RFC 8869, but defines no quality metrics, and passing the tests does not show an algorithm is free of risk.

today: RFC 8868 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It supplies network parameters and traffic models for the test cases in RFC 8867 and RFC 8869.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This memo gives guidelines for evaluating new congestion control algorithms for interactive point-to-point real-time media. The requirements for the algorithms are in RFC 8836. It builds on RFC 5033 and RFC 5166, and expects proposed algorithms to operate within the envelope of the circuit breakers in RFC 8083.

It provides only the broad set of network parameters and traffic models. The minimal requirement is to present results for the Basic Test Cases of RFC 8867, and proponents may also present results for the wireless scenarios of RFC 8869.

No quality metrics are defined, because quality of experience metrics vary between media types and evolve. There is consensus that each algorithm should still show it is useful for interactive video, using real codecs, video sequences and state-of-the-art quality metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the rulebook for the test course. It does not say how good a video looks, only how to run a fair test.

sections.title: Metrics and the RTP Log Format
sections.content:
Each experiment is expected to log every incoming and outgoing packet, either inside the application or with packet capture such as tcpdump or Wireshark. The log has one line per packet with the send or receive timestamp, RTP payload type, SSRC, RTP sequence number, RTP timestamp, marker bit and payload size in bytes.

From the logs, the metrics include sending rate, receiver rate and goodput (measured at 200ms intervals), packets and bytes sent and received, packet delay, packets lost or discarded, and post-repair loss when retransmission or FEC is used. Experiments must also report fairness, as ratios of average throughput between the RTP streams and, when present, cross traffic. The throughput interval should be set at a few values, for example 1 s, 5 s and 20 s.

As a general guideline, the ratio between congestion-controlled RTP flows of the same priority and similar path RTT should be bounded between 0.333 and 3. Other metrics are convergence time, instability or oscillation of the sending rate, and bandwidth utilization.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet gets written in a notebook. Afterwards you can work out how fast things went, how long they took, and whether two calls shared fairly.

sections.title: Network Parameters
sections.content:
Implementors are encouraged to choose settings from set values. One-way propagation delay covers very low (0-1 ms), low (50 ms), high (150 ms) and extreme (300 ms) latency. End-to-end loss is chosen from 0%, 1%, 5%, 10% and 20%.

Routers should use drop-tail queues, and AQM experiments are encouraged but not mandatory. Queue length is measured as the time taken to drain the FIFO queue: QoS-aware (70 ms), nominal (300-500 ms) and buffer-bloated (1000-2000 ms).

For losses, independent random losses must be used as the minimal model, and correlated models such as Gilbert-Elliott may also be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: The test course has short and long roads, roads that drop some packages, and waiting lines of different lengths, so the idea gets tried in easy and hard conditions.

sections.title: Jitter Models
sections.content:
The RFC uses the term Packet Delay Variation (PDV) instead of jitter, because jitter is an overloaded term. It defines two bounded PDV models. Random Bounded PDV (RBPDV) is presented for information only and can reorder packets when the spread of delays exceeds the gap between two sent packets.

NR-BPDV (no-reordering bounded PDV) must be used in the evaluation. It adjusts the delays so that a packet is never emitted earlier than the previous packet plus its serialization delay, which models a per-flow queue and delays caused by devices such as middleboxes.

For both models, the delay offset is recommended to follow a truncated Gaussian distribution with a standard deviation of 5 ms and a bound of 3 standard deviations.
sections.plainLanguage: Packages sometimes arrive a bit early or late. The test adds this wobble on purpose, but never lets one package overtake the one in front of it.

sections.title: Traffic Models
sections.content:
Long-lived TCP flows have an infinite amount of data to send. Short TCP flows are modeled as 30 connections starting at the same time fetching small amounts of data (30-50 KB), with idle periods between bursts drawn from an exponential distribution with a mean of 10 seconds. Experiments should try a range of TCP schemes, especially CUBIC, and must document which schemes and parameters were used.

For RTP video, RFC 8593 describes two models, one statistical and one based on video traces. The recommended minimum test sequences are Foreman (CIF) and FourPeople (720p), stitched together repeatedly until the desired length is reached.

Background UDP is a constant bit rate flow, with the packet size typically the path MTU (default 1500 bytes). Protocols such as QUIC that run over UDP are expected to behave like the TCP flows.
sections.plainLanguage: The call must share the road with other traffic: long downloads, bursts of small web pages and a steady stream of background data.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document specifies evaluation criteria, so it is not itself subject to security considerations, but the algorithms evaluated may be. Succeeding in all the tests may suffice for a comparison but must not be read as showing the protocol is free of risks when deployed on the Internet.

Evaluations are carried out in controlled environments with limited numbers of flows, so careful design is advised to avoid contributing to local congestion collapse. The tests do not check for malicious use such as faked, dropped, replicated or modified congestion signals. The protocol specifications themselves must check authenticity, integrity and plausibility of received signals.
sections.plainLanguage: Passing the test course does not make an idea safe in the real world, and the course does not check for cheaters.
